tutorials.title: Chart the grid with one prop
tutorials.description: Add charting to SvGrid and a panel charts the rows on screen: pick a type and a group-by, click a bar to filter the grid, open the builder.

transcript.text: Add the charting prop and the grid grows a chart panel. It charts the rows on screen, so filtering or sorting redraws it.
Pick a type, a group-by column and the aggregate.
Click a bar and the grid filters to that category. Clear filter brings the rows back.
Build opens a gallery with a live thumbnail per type, and a Format tab for titles, axes and series.
Everything here is a config field or an API call, and it round-trips through the saved view.

tutorials.title: Excel-style filter menu in SvGrid
tutorials.description: Set filterMode to menu and every column gets an Excel-style filter: a searchable value list with checkboxes that re-filters the grid as you tick.

transcript.text: Set filterMode to menu, and each column header shows a filter button on hover. Click it to open the menu.
The menu lists every distinct value. Untick one, and the grid re-filters right away.
Long value lists have a search box. Type a few letters to narrow the choices.
Done closes the menu. The filtered column keeps its marker, and Clear filter in the same menu resets it.

tutorials.title: Excel-style fill handle in SvGrid
tutorials.description: Select a range, drag the corner fill handle, and SvGrid continues the series: numbers, weekdays and dates, or a plain copy for a single cell.

transcript.text: With cell selection on, every range gets a fill handle at its corner. Select the two seed cells of the numeric series.
Drag the handle to the right. Ten and twenty become a series in steps of ten, filled as far as you drag.
Weekdays and dates continue the same way. A single seed switches to copy mode and repeats the value.
Every filled cell goes through the normal edit pipeline, so validation and change tracking still apply.

tutorials.title: A financial chart workbench in Svelte
tutorials.description: Candlesticks with volume, RSI and MACD panes and Bollinger bands: indicator chips, Ctrl + wheel zoom every pane follows, range presets, and the grid panel.

transcript.text: A year of sessions as candles, with volume, RSI and MACD panes under the price and Bollinger bands on it.
Toggle an indicator chip and its pane comes and goes.
Ctrl plus wheel zooms the price, and every pane follows.
A range preset jumps to the last month.
The grid's own panel draws the same rows: Candlestick picked, indicator chips, the builder, and the link toggle.

tutorials.title: Inline editing in SvGrid
tutorials.description: Turn on inline editing with one prop, edit cells with text, dropdown and date editors, and track pending changes before you save.

transcript.text: Inline editing in SvGrid is one prop. Set enableInlineEditing and double-click any cell to start.
Type a new value and press Enter to commit it.
Columns pick their own editor. Department is a list, so double-clicking it opens a dropdown, and one click picks the value.
Every change is tracked. The pending edits card counts what is not saved yet, and Save changes commits the batch.

tutorials.title: Install the SvGrid spreadsheet
tutorials.description: Add an Excel-style spreadsheet to a Svelte app: install the enterprise package, pass a workbook to SvSheet, and type formulas into a ribbon-driven sheet.
tutorials.anchor: The examples on this page share one setup

transcript.text: The spreadsheet ships in the enterprise package. Install it next to the grid; it runs unlicensed for evaluation.
A workbook is plain data: sheets with a name and a cells matrix. Formulas are strings that start with an equals sign.
Hand it to SvSheet. That is the whole API.
The result is the full surface: a ribbon, the name box and formula bar, lettered columns, sheet tabs and a status bar, with the totals already computed.
It behaves like a spreadsheet. Type a formula into a cell, press Enter, and the value appears while the formula bar keeps the source.
Every Excel shortcut, fill handle, number formats, conditional formatting and xlsx import and export come with it. The docs list the whole surface.

tutorials.title: SvGrid Studio: database to CRUD app
tutorials.description: Scaffold a SvelteKit data app from the command line or the visual designer: tables in, a list, an edit form and a record page per table out.
tutorials.anchor: ## Guided path - answer a few questions, get the app

transcript.text: SvGrid Studio turns tables into a SvelteKit app. From the command line, one create command scaffolds a runnable app with sample tables.
Point init at a real database and it reads the tables, then writes a list, an edit form and a record page for each one.
The same generator runs in the browser. The designer opens with a wizard: start from sample data, your own database, or blank.
Pick a dataset, choose which pages each table gets, and open the app.
Two tables became six screens: an overview with a KPI and a chart, a list, a manage page and a detail page per table, all on the canvas to rearrange.
Preview runs the app as a user sees it: the grid, the new record button, the navigation.
Generate app writes the SvelteKit project: twenty-seven files, typed schemas, routes and a CI workflow. Download the zip or open it in StackBlitz.

tutorials.title: Install SvGrid
tutorials.description: Add the Svelte 5 data grid to a project: one npm package, one import, a data array and a columns array, and a styled table renders.

transcript.text: SvGrid is one npm package. In an existing Svelte 5 project, install it and you are done with setup.
Starting from scratch? The create command scaffolds a working project with the grid already wired.
Either way, a grid is a component, a data array and a columns array. Import SvGrid and describe the rows.
Columns map a field to a header. Then render the component with both.
Save, and the dev server shows a styled table with keyboard navigation, selection and a focus ring, all out of the box.
Sorting, filtering, editing and the rest are features you switch on next. The docs at svgrid.com take it from here.

tutorials.title: Kanban board mode in SvGrid
tutorials.description: Render the same SvGrid as a Kanban board with one board prop: lanes from a status field, drag and drop between lanes, WIP limits, and a table view.

transcript.text: One board prop turns the grid into a Kanban board. Lanes come from the status field, and every card is a row.
Drag a card from Backlog into Review.
The drop writes the new status back to the row, so the data and the board never disagree. In progress carries a WIP limit and refuses a card past it.
Switch to Table, and the same rows show as a grid, with the card you moved already in Review.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 1: install and your first grid
tutorials.description: Lesson one of the SvGrid course: install the package, write a twenty-line component, and get a styled, keyboard-navigable table.
tutorials.anchor: ## What you got out of the box

transcript.text: Welcome to lesson one. By the end of it you will have a working data grid in a Svelte 5 project, and you will understand every line that put it there.
SvGrid is a single npm package. There is no CLI step and nothing to copy into your project: you install it and import from it.
It needs Svelte 5, because the grid is built on runes. If you are starting from nothing, the create command scaffolds a project with the grid already wired up.
Now the component. Import SvGrid, and import the GridColumns type as well. That type is what makes the column list check itself against your rows.
Your data is a plain array of plain objects. No store, no wrapper, no adapter. If you already have rows in your app, they are already in the right shape.

Columns are the other half. Each one maps a field on your row to a header the user reads. Because the array is typed as GridColumns of Person, a typo in a field name is a compile error, not a blank column.
Then render the component with both. That is the whole API for a basic grid: data in, columns in.
Save, and the dev server shows this. A real table element, with a header row and your three rows in it.
You did not ask for any of this, but you got it: click a cell and it takes focus, arrow keys move between cells, Home and End jump to the ends of a row. That is the ARIA grid pattern, on by default.

What you do not have yet is sorting, filtering or paging. Those are switched on deliberately, so a grid you never configured stays small in your bundle. Lesson two puts your own data in, and lesson three turns those features on.
The code from this lesson is on the page linked below, and it runs there too. See you in lesson two.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 10: going to production
tutorials.description: Lesson ten: virtualization, the accessibility you already have, server-rendered markup, and the TypeScript habit that prevents blank columns.

transcript.text: Your grid works. This last lesson is the review a colleague would give it: the four things that decide whether it survives contact with real data and real users.

First, scale. Virtualization is on by default, so only the rows in view have DOM nodes. Fifty thousand rows by seventy-seven columns scroll in both directions, and the count of nodes stays roughly the same as it was with ten rows.
What you do have to give it is a height. A grid inside a container with no height cannot know what is on screen, and that is the single most common reason a large table feels slow.

Second, accessibility, which you mostly already have. It is a real table element carrying the ARIA grid pattern, so a screen reader announces rows and columns, and every cell is reachable from the keyboard.
What is on you is the rest of the page: a label on the grid, contrast that passes, and not removing the focus ring. There is a high-contrast preset in the box if procurement asks.

Third, the markup server-renders, so a viewport of real rows reaches the browser before hydration. And fourth, the habit that costs nothing: type the column array as GridColumns of your row. A bare GridColumns widens the row and stops checking field names, and a typo becomes a blank column nobody notices until a user does.

That is the course. You can build a grid, shape its columns, sort and filter it, edit it, group it, theme it, feed it from a server and ship it. Everything past this point is a feature you turn on when you need it, and the demos on the site show each one running.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 2: your data, your columns
tutorials.description: Lesson two of the SvGrid course: put your own row type in, keep it reactive, then set headers, widths and currency, percent and date formats.

transcript.text: In lesson one the rows were made up. In this one they are yours, they stay reactive, and the columns start looking like a real application.
Start from your own row type. The grid never asks you to convert anything: whatever shape your records have, that is the shape it takes. Declare the array with the state rune and it stays reactive.
Columns map a field to a header, and width fixes one that would otherwise stretch. Then a plain function that pushes a record onto the array.
Watch what happens when that button runs. Pushing onto the array is all it does, and the grid follows, because the rows are a rune and not a copy the grid took at startup.
Now formatting. This is the same page of the docs, a few blocks further down, and it is the thing people most often do by hand and regret.

A currency format, a percent, a date. Each one renders the value for the reader and leaves your data alone, which matters because sorting and exporting both use the raw number underneath, not the string on screen.

One habit worth forming: type the column array as GridColumns of your row type. The compiler then checks every field name against the row, so a typo is a build error instead of an empty column nobody notices.
Both files are on the page below, and they run there too. See you in lesson three.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 3: sorting, filtering and paging
tutorials.description: Lesson three of the SvGrid course: switch on sorting, filtering, grouping and pagination with boolean props, and see what each one does to the same table.

transcript.text: Your grid renders. It does not sort, filter or page yet, and that is deliberate. This lesson turns those on and explains the trade the library is making for you.
Here is a wider row type and a realistic set of records, the kind of table you would actually ship. Nothing new yet.
Columns, with a currency format on salary from the last lesson.

And now the part that matters. Sortable, filterable, editable, groupable, pageable. Each is one boolean, and each one pulls in only the code that feature needs, which is why a grid you never configured stays small.
That is the whole file: the row type, the records, the columns, and the component with those five words on it. Nothing else is configured, and nothing is hidden above the fold.
Click a header and it sorts. Click again for descending, and a third time to clear it and get your original order back.
Shift-click a second header to sort by two columns at once: department first, then name inside each department.
The funnel next to each header is filtering, switched on by that same one word. How it looks is a choice, and the next screen has the version most people want.

Five rows will not show you paging, so here is the same set of props over five thousand. Filterable on its own gives you a menu per header; filter mode row puts an input under each header instead, and it narrows the table as you type.
And the pager cuts what is left into pages, with the range and the count kept honest as the filter changes them. None of this needed a callback from you.

Those five booleans are a shorthand. When you need finer control, register the features explicitly with tableFeatures and pass them in, which is the same machinery with the wiring exposed; the docs page below shows both forms side by side. Lesson four lets people change the table.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 4: editing rows, and validating them
tutorials.description: Lesson four of the SvGrid course: make cells editable, pick an editor per column, and use validate with rejectInvalid so bad input never reaches your data.

transcript.text: A table people can only read is half a feature. This lesson makes it editable, and then makes it refuse the edits that should not happen.
The same reactive rows as before. Three people, three fields.
Each column picks its editor. Text for a name, number for an age. The editor is chosen per column, so the user gets the right control instead of a text box for everything.
Then validate. It runs as the cell is edited and returns a message when the value is wrong. Pair it with rejectInvalid and the edit is refused outright rather than written and cleaned up later.
Double-click a cell to edit it, type, and press Enter to commit. That is the whole gesture, and it is the one spreadsheet users already know.

Now an email that is not one. Validate runs as you type, and hovering the cell tells the user what is wrong. Press Enter and rejectInvalid refuses the commit outright: the value is still the old one. Your row object is never touched by something you would have to clean up later.

Undo with control zed, save in batches through the grid API, or hand every commit to your server. The editing pages in the docs cover each of those. Lesson five is selection, and doing something with the rows the user picked.
The file is on the page below and you can edit it there too. See you in lesson five.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 5: selection and bulk actions
tutorials.description: Lesson five of the SvGrid course: add row checkboxes, give the grid a stable row id, and float a bulk-action bar over the rows the user picked.

transcript.text: Selecting rows is easy. Knowing which rows are selected after a sort, a filter or a refresh is the part that catches people out, and it comes down to one prop.
A small backlog of tasks and the columns to show them.

Three things on the component. showRowSelection adds the checkbox column. selectionBar floats the action bar. And getRowId is the one that matters: it tells the grid what identifies a row, so a selection survives sorting, filtering and new data arriving. Without it the grid falls back to position, and position changes.
Tick a couple of rows and the bar appears with a live count and the actions you defined. It stays out of the way until there is something to act on.
Now sort the table while those rows are ticked. The same three stay selected, because the grid is tracking ids rather than row numbers.
Over server data the same idea scales: select-all becomes a rule, every row except these, rather than a list of ids the browser would have to hold. Lesson six groups the rows and adds totals.
The file is on the page below. See you in lesson six.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 6: grouping and totals
tutorials.description: Lesson six of the SvGrid course: group rows by a column, average and sum per group with the aggregate option, and add a summary row for the whole table.

transcript.text: Once a table has more than a screenful of rows, people stop reading it and start asking it questions. Grouping and totals are how it answers.
The same people as before, with a department and a city to group by, and a salary worth adding up.

Two options do the work here. Aggregate says what a group header shows for that column: an average age, a summed salary. Summary does the same thing for the whole table at the bottom. Both read the raw value, so a formatted currency still adds up correctly.
Then groupBy on the component names the starting grouping, and groupable lets the user change it later.
Read it back whole: the same people, one column list with the aggregate and summary options on it, and groupBy on the component. That is everything this needs.
Every department is a group header carrying its own totals, and the row at the bottom totals the table. Open one and the people inside are ordinary rows: still sortable, still editable, still yours.

Grouping is part of the row model rather than a display trick, which is why the same thing works over server data: the server returns the groups and the grid asks for a group's rows only when someone opens it. Lesson seven makes all of this look like your product.
The file is on the page below. See you in lesson seven.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 7: themes, dark mode and density
tutorials.description: Lesson seven of the SvGrid course: set the CSS custom properties yourself, flip dark mode with one attribute, and change row density with a prop.

transcript.text: A grid that looks like a grid library is a grid that never ships. Theming here is CSS custom properties, not utility classes and not a config object.

Twenty presets ship with the package, and importing one stylesheet is the whole setup. What a preset sets is a list of custom properties, which means you can set them yourself when one is close but not right. Same five people as before.

A wrapper, and a handful of properties on it. Background, text, border, the header colours, the accent, the hover. They cascade like any other custom property, so this theme is scoped to this one grid rather than the page.
The whole file, so nothing is hidden: the rows, the columns, a wrapper around the grid, and the properties on that wrapper.
Here is that file running. Nine declarations, and nothing about the grid was configured to accept them.
Density is separate from colour, and it is the setting people actually argue about. Row height is a prop, so the compact table and the comfortable one are the same component with one number changed.

Dark mode is not a second stylesheet you maintain. Every preset declares a light palette and a dark one, and an attribute on the document element picks which is live. Every surface follows, including the parts you never styled.
The density control here is the same row height prop behind a dropdown, which is what it usually becomes: a preference you save per user rather than a decision you make once for everybody.
The theme builder on the site edits these tokens live and hands you the CSS at the end. Every property is listed on the page below. See you in lesson eight.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 8: data from a server
tutorials.description: Lesson eight of the SvGrid course: move sorting, filtering and paging to the backend, send one request per change, and cancel the one that is now stale.

transcript.text: Everything so far held every row in memory. That works to tens of thousands of rows. Past that, the sorting and filtering have to move to the server, and the grid has to ask for what it needs.
The state the grid hands you is small: which column is sorted, which filters are set, which page you are on. Keep those in runes.

Then one function that turns that state into a request. Notice the abort controller: when the user types another letter, the request already in flight is cancelled, so a slow earlier response cannot overwrite a newer one. That race is the most common bug in a server-backed table.
An effect reruns it whenever sort, filters or page change, and the component passes the rows down with the total, so the pager knows how many pages there are without counting rows it never received.
Here is that pattern running against a real endpoint. Sorting goes to the server and comes back sorted; typing in the search box is debounced, so one request goes out rather than one per keystroke.
The loading state lives on the rows rather than as a spinner over the page, so the header and the controls stay usable while the next page arrives.
Past a million rows there is a dedicated row model that lazily loads groups and blocks; it is linked from the page below. Lesson nine puts all of this in a SvelteKit app.

tutorials.title: Learn SvGrid 9: SvelteKit end to end
tutorials.description: Lesson nine of the SvGrid course: query in a load function, hand the rows to the page, and get real server-rendered HTML instead of an empty shell.

transcript.text: SvelteKit gives you a place to put the query that is already on the server. The grid does not need to know about any of it: it takes an array.
There is a SvelteKit template, so the whole app is two commands. If you have a project already, installing the package is enough.
The load function runs on the server. Your database credentials are already there, so the query belongs there too, and the browser never sees it.
The page takes what that returned and hands it straight to the grid. Type the columns against your row type, as in lesson two, and the compiler checks the field names for you.
Here is a grid over a real endpoint, which is what your page becomes once the load function points at a database instead of a demo API.
The part worth knowing: the server HTML contains a viewport of real rows, not an empty container waiting for hydration. A crawler sees data, and a reader sees the table before the JavaScript arrives.
URL-driven sorting and form actions for edits are on the page below. One lesson to go.

tutorials.title: Master detail rows in SvGrid
tutorials.description: Expand a row into a nested detail grid with two props, isDetailRow and renderDetailRow: the detail is a real row, so scrolling and virtualization still apply.

transcript.text: Master detail in SvGrid is two props. isDetailRow marks a row as a detail, and renderDetailRow draws whatever you like inside it.
Click the chevron on an account to expand its call records, a nested grid with its own sorting.
Expand as many as you like. Each detail is a real row in the grid, so keyboard navigation and virtualization keep working.
Click the chevron again to collapse. The expanded set is plain state, so you can save and restore it.

tutorials.title: One million rows in SvGrid
tutorials.description: Scroll a one million row Svelte data grid: row virtualization draws only the rows in view, with sorting, filtering and editing still on.

transcript.text: This SvGrid holds one million rows, generated in the browser, with sorting, filtering and inline editing switched on.
Rows are virtualized, so only the ones in view are drawn. Scroll, and the frame rate stays flat.
Jump anywhere in the set. The row numbers show the scale, and the grid keeps every row reachable.
Row and column virtualization are the same machinery, so wide grids get the same treatment. Nothing to configure.

tutorials.title: An accessible data grid, not a div soup
tutorials.description: SvGrid renders the WAI-ARIA grid pattern on a real table: keyboard navigation everywhere, a command palette, a cheat sheet, and a high-contrast preset.

transcript.text: Most grids are a pile of divs. This one is a table with the ARIA grid pattern on it.
Arrow keys move the active cell, Home and End jump to the row edges, Control Home goes to the corner, and the focus ring follows.
Control K opens a command palette over the grid, and Control slash shows every shortcut the app has bound.
And a high-contrast preset ships with it, for the procurement checklist that asks.
There is a published conformance report to hand to whoever asks for one. Accessibility at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Alert rules your users write themselves
tutorials.description: Let users define rules over grid data at run time: raise a toast, tint a row, flash a cell, watch a whole-table total, or veto an edit that breaks a limit.

transcript.text: The rule a user needs tomorrow is never the one you shipped today. So let them write it.
A live trading desk with rules watching it. When a row matches, the rule raises a toast, tints the row or flashes the cell.
Rules can watch an aggregate rather than a row: a total, an average, a count across the whole table.
And a validation rule runs on edit, so a change that breaks a limit is refused before it lands.
Rules are stored as data, so users keep their own and you ship nothing. Alerts at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: A calendar view for grid rows
tutorials.description: The SvGrid scheduler prop: month, week, day and agenda over the same rows, resource timelines, and a full calendar client built from the parts.

transcript.text: Events are rows with a start and an end. The calendar is one more view of the grid.
Month, week, day and agenda over the same rows, with drag to move and resize, and every change flowing back to the row.
Timelines put resources in rows and time across: teams, rooms, machines.
Compose it with the dock layout and a navigation pane, and you have a full calendar client.
Recurring events, drafts, ICS import and export, resource views. Calendars at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Charts that read the grid
tutorials.description: SvGrid charting: a panel that draws the rows on screen and filters the grid on click, thirty chart types from one dataset, financial panes with synced zoom.

transcript.text: The chart is not a second library. It reads the rows the grid is showing.
Add the charting prop and pick a type. Click a bar and the grid filters to that category.
Thirty chart types from one dataset: bars, lines, areas, pies, funnels, candlesticks, heat maps and more.
Financial panes with indicators, and a zoom that keeps every pane in step.
Export to PNG or SVG, drop a chart on a dashboard, or chart a pivot or a sheet range. Charts at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Columns your users can rearrange
tutorials.description: Pin, reorder, resize and group columns in SvGrid, and dock a tool panel so users can show, hide and group them without you writing a settings screen.

transcript.text: A wide table is only useful if the columns that matter stay put. SvGrid gives that control to the user.
Pin a column left or right and it stays while the rest slide under it. Pinning is a column option, or a choice in the header menu.
Drag a header to reorder, drag its edge to resize, and both land in the column state you can save and restore.
Switch on the tool panel and users get the whole thing themselves: show and hide columns, reorder them, group by one, all from a docked sidebar.
The whole layout is one object you can store per user and restore on load. Columns at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Excel habits on a data grid
tutorials.description: The gestures spreadsheet users bring with them, on SvGrid: the filter menu with a value list, the fill handle, and Excel keyboard shortcuts.

transcript.text: Your users learned spreadsheets first. SvGrid meets them where they are.
Every column gets the filter menu they know: a value list with counts, a search box and conditions.
The fill handle continues a series: numbers, dates and weekdays, or repeats a single value.
Turn on sheet mode and the keyboard follows: Control plus an arrow jumps to the edge of the data, Shift extends the selection.
Paste special, find and replace, move a range, undo. All of it on the grid you already have. Demos at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Export a Svelte grid to Excel, PDF and print
tutorials.description: Export the grid the user is looking at: XLSX with live formulas, PDF, CSV, a printable view, and a password-protected workbook, all from the same API.

transcript.text: Every internal tool gets the same request: can I have this in Excel. Here is the answer.
One call exports what the grid is showing. Sort or filter first and the file follows, because it reads the view, not the raw array.
Currency, dates and percentages land formatted, not as raw numbers, and print opens the same view ready for paper.
A total column can go out as a live SUM, so the workbook recalculates in Excel instead of freezing your numbers.
CSV ships in the free core; Excel, PDF and protected workbooks come with the enterprise pack. Export at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Four ways to filter a Svelte data grid
tutorials.description: Filtering in SvGrid: a quick filter row under the headers, the Excel-style value list, a visual condition builder, and set filters over large value lists.

transcript.text: Every team filters differently, so SvGrid ships four ways to do it on the same columns.
The filter row sits under the headers. Each cell knows its column type, and the funnel picks the operator.
The column menu is the Excel-style one: a searchable value list with counts, ticked and unticked.
For the hard questions there is a visual builder: nested AND and OR conditions across columns, saved as a query your users can reuse.
The same filter model serializes to the server when the data is too big for the browser. Filtering at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Headless first: bring your own markup
tutorials.description: SvGrid is an engine plus a renderer. Use createSvGrid for sorting, filtering and row models in your own table markup, and the virtualizer for 50,000 rows.

transcript.text: Sometimes you want the logic, not the look. SvGrid separates the two.
This is a hand-written table, not the grid component. createSvGrid does the sorting and the filtering; the markup is yours.
The virtualizer is separate too: it tells you which rows are in view and where to put them, so fifty thousand rows cost about twenty nodes.
Same package, same row model, whichever half you use. Headless at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Edit in place, every field type
tutorials.description: Inline editing on SvGrid: text, dropdown and date editors, a validate hook per column, and editors whose options depend on other cells.

transcript.text: Editing is one prop, and every column brings the right editor with it.
Text, dropdowns and dates, in place: double-click, type or pick, press Enter. Pending edits are counted until you save.
A validate hook per column rejects bad input with a message before it ever reaches your data.
Editors can depend on each other. Pick a region, and the country list narrows to match.
Undo, cascading options, validation and batch saves, with one prop. Docs at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Kanban boards on your rows
tutorials.description: The SvGrid board prop: cards are rows, lanes are a field, swimlanes cross them with a second field, WIP limits hold, and cards get rich by config.

transcript.text: Cards are rows. Lanes are a field. The board is a prop on the grid you already have.
Drag a card between lanes and the row behind it changes status.
Swimlanes cross the lanes with a second field, here the assignee, and a WIP limit refuses a card past the line.
Cards get rich by config alone: labels, avatars, sub-task progress, comments and attachments, no template code.
Virtualized lanes, keyboard drag and drop, filters and card menus, epics with stories. Ten demos at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Live data without the flicker
tutorials.description: Real-time on SvGrid: a ticking price feed that flashes what moved, sensor rows regrouped on the fly, and a server-side transaction stream applied in batches.

transcript.text: Prices, sensors, transactions. Rows that change every second, in a grid that does not blink.
A ticking feed updates cells in place and flashes what moved, while sorting and filtering stay applied.
Sensor rows with thresholds driving the colours and sparklines tracking the trend, regrouped by status on the fly.
Server-side too: a transaction stream applies inserts, updates and removes to a row model the browser does not own, in batches.
Batched transactions keep the frame rate whatever the feed does. Real-time at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: A million rows in the browser
tutorials.description: SvGrid virtualizes rows and columns: one million rows sorted, filtered and grouped in the browser, and 100 columns that scroll both ways.

transcript.text: How many rows can a Svelte grid hold before it slows down? Let us find out.
One million rows, generated in the browser. Scroll anywhere; only the rows in view are drawn.
Group them by department and the same million rows fold into groups, still in place.
Columns virtualize too. Fifty thousand rows by seventy-seven columns scroll in both directions without a stutter.
The numbers are on the benchmarks page, with the harness that produced them. Start at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Pivot tables in the browser
tutorials.description: SvPivotDesigner: drag fields into rows, columns and values, flip the same layout to a chart, or dock the designer beside a flat grid and switch pivot mode.

transcript.text: A pivot table used to mean exporting to a spreadsheet. Not anymore.
Drag fields into rows, columns and values and the pivot recomputes on the spot.
Flip to Chart and the same layout draws itself.
Or dock the designer beside a flat grid and flip pivot mode: same rows, two views, no second data source.
Subtotals and grand totals, saved presets, export, and a server mode for millions of rows. Pivot at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Connect a Svelte data grid to your API
tutorials.description: Point SvGrid at a REST endpoint: server sort, filter and paging over a live public API, cursor pagination, and a loading state that does not flicker.

transcript.text: A demo with hard-coded rows proves nothing. This one is talking to a real endpoint over the network.
Every page turn is an HTTP request. The grid asks for the slice it needs, and the adapter maps your response shape to rows and a total.
Cursor APIs work the same way: the grid keeps the cursor your backend returned and asks for what follows it.
Sorting and searching go the same way, debounced, with the loading state on the rows rather than a spinner over the page.
REST, GraphQL, SQL or Supabase, it is one function you implement. Server data at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Groups, trees and detail rows
tutorials.description: Three ways SvGrid nests rows: grouping with aggregates, tree data from a parent field, and master detail rows that open a nested grid.

transcript.text: Flat rows are the exception. SvGrid nests them three ways.
Group by any column with a sum or an average per group, and switch the grouping at run time.
Tree data: point the grid at a parent field and rows become a hierarchy, with expanders and indent.
Master detail: a row opens a detail row, here a nested grid with its own sorting.
Three props on one row model, virtualized and keyboard-navigable. Details at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Select rows, act on them in bulk
tutorials.description: Selection in SvGrid: row checkboxes, a floating bulk-action bar, spreadsheet range selection, and dragging a selected block to move or copy it.

transcript.text: Selecting rows is only half the job. What the user does next is the other half.
Tick a few rows and a bar floats over the grid with the actions you defined, and a live count of what is selected.
Cell selection works like a spreadsheet: drag a range, then grab its border and move the block somewhere else.
And the corner handle fills a series across the range, the way a spreadsheet does.
Over server data, select-all becomes a rule rather than a list of ids, so it works past a million rows. More at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: The Server-Side Row Model
tutorials.description: A million rows that stay on the server: SvGrid turns scrolling, grouping, tree expansion and pivoting into requests your backend answers.

transcript.text: When the data cannot fit in the browser, the grid asks the server for exactly what it shows.
Scrolling fetches blocks on demand. Grouping is a request too: the server returns the groups, and each opens lazily.
A file tree the grid never holds whole. Expanding a folder is one call with the folder as the parent.
Even the pivot runs on the server: one request per layout. Expand a region and the pivot repeats per country beneath it.
One getRows function against any backend, and a planner that turns each request into SQL. Details at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: A headless table in Svelte
tutorials.description: Use the grid engine without its renderer: createSvGrid gives you rows, headers, sorting and pagination, and you write the table markup and the CSS yourself.

transcript.text: Sometimes you want the logic and not the look. You have a design system already, or the markup has to be a particular shape, and a component that renders its own table is the wrong tool. This is the other half of SvGrid: the engine on its own, with no renderer attached.

It comes from a separate entry point, slash core, so none of the rendering code is in your bundle. You describe the data and the columns the same way you would for the component: a row type, an array of plain objects, and a column per field.

Then createSvGrid builds the table instance. The row models are the part worth understanding: a model is a stage in the pipeline, and you opt into each one. Here there is only the core model, so the engine hands back your rows in order and does nothing else to them.

And this is the part a rendering component would never let you write. Your own table element, your own classes, your own cells. The engine gives you header groups and rows; what they look like is entirely yours.

Sixty lines, and the result is a plain HTML table. No grid stylesheet, no wrapper divs, no class names you did not choose. If your design system has a table component already, this is how you keep it and still get sorting, filtering, grouping and pagination underneath.

Sorting is a second row model and a piece of state you own. Add the sorted model, keep the sorting array in a rune, and put an onclick on your own header. Clicking cycles that column: ascending, descending, then back to the order your data arrived in. And because the state is an array rather than a single column, clicking a second header adds to the sort instead of replacing it, so multi-column sorting falls out of the same three lines.

Pagination is the same move again. Add the paginated model and the engine hands back one page at a time, with the page count and the controls left to you. And notice this one is not a table at all. It is a list, because nothing in the engine knows or cares what you draw: it gives you rows, and the markup is a decision you make per screen.

Virtualization is separate too, and it is the reason this is worth doing rather than writing the loop by hand. The virtualizer tells you which rows are in view and the offset to put them at. You still write the row markup; you just write fifty of them instead of fifty thousand. Scroll it and the DOM node count holds steady while the data under it does not. Doing that yourself is where most hand-rolled tables quietly fall over, because it is not the first thousand rows that hurt, it is the scroll position arithmetic when the rows are different heights.

The table is not the only thing with a headless half. There are around twenty more: a calendar, a combobox, an autocomplete, a tags input, a slider, a tree. Each one is a function that owns the state and the keyboard behaviour and hands you the parts to render. That is the part people underestimate. A date picker is two days of work if you write the markup, and two weeks if you also have to get arrow keys, page up and down, home and end, the month roll-over and the screen reader announcements right. This gives you the second part and leaves you the first.

Same package either way. Import from slash core and you get the engine with none of the renderer; import from the package root and you get a grid that draws itself, with the same row models underneath. You can start headless and switch later, or use both in one app. The docs page below builds this table from scratch.

tutorials.title: A Kanban board in Svelte, from an array of objects
tutorials.description: Give the Svelte 5 data grid a board prop and your rows become cards in lanes: drag to change a field, swimlanes, WIP limits, and the same data as a table.

transcript.text: Most board libraries ask you to model a board: lanes, cards, an order per lane. This one does not. You already have rows, and a lane is just a field on them.
Here is the same grid twice. As a table it is rows and columns. Switch it to board and each row becomes a card, grouped into lanes by whichever field you name.

Move a card and the row behind it changes. You can drag it, or focus it and move it from the keyboard: Space to pick it up, arrows to move it, Space to drop. The board is a view of the data, so there is no second copy to keep in step.
The card is yours. This is a sales pipeline: the lanes are deal stages, the card is a snippet you wrote, and the lane header totals the deals inside it as they move.
Cross the lanes with a swimlane and you get a grid of both: status across, priority down. Search filters the cards in place, and a lane can refuse work past a limit.
Point it at a child field and a card carries its own children, so an epic shows its stories without a second board underneath.

It is one prop on a grid that is MIT on npm, it keeps your row type the whole way through, and the board, the table and the chart are the same component. The docs page below has the code from all of this.

tutorials.title: A pivot table and an OLAP cube in Svelte
tutorials.description: Cross-tab your rows without a second library: a pivot from four lines, a drag-and-drop designer, pivot mode on the grid you already have, and a cube browser.

transcript.text: A pivot table used to mean exporting to a spreadsheet. The data is already in the browser, in a grid that knows the shape of every row, so the sensible place to pivot it is right there. This is what that looks like in Svelte, starting from the smallest version and ending at a cube browser.

Here is the smallest pivot there is. The same rows you would put in a table, and one more prop describing the shape you want: which fields go down the side, which go across the top, and what to aggregate in the middle.

That is the whole configuration. Rows, columns, values, and an aggregation per value. The engine groups, aggregates and lays out the cross-tab, and the result is still a grid, so it sorts, scrolls and exports like one.

Change the shape and the numbers follow. Add a second field down the side and you get a nested cross-tab, with subtotals at each level, because the aggregation is computed per group rather than summed from the cells above it.

Most of the time the person who wants the pivot is not the person who wrote the code, so there is a designer. Fields down one side, three wells on the other: rows, columns and values. Tick a field and it joins the layout in the well that suits its type, and the cross-tab recomputes on the spot.

And you do not need a separate component for it. A grid you already have flips into pivot mode with one switch: the flat rows become the cross-tab, the designer docks beside it, and flipping back returns the table you started with.

Push it further and you get a cube browser: dimensions nested down the side, measures across the top, and a tabular layout an analyst recognises immediately. Expand a dimension and the level below it appears with its own subtotals. Every number here is computed in the browser from the rows you handed it. There is no cube server behind this, no query language to learn, and no second dependency in the bundle. The practical consequence is that the thing your users asked for, the one that normally means a BI tool and a nightly job, is a prop on a component in your own app, against data you already loaded, behind your own auth.

A cross-tab is already the shape a chart wants: categories down one axis, series across the other, a number in each cell. So the same layout drives a chart without you restating any of it. Re-pivot and the chart follows, because it is reading the pivot result rather than a copy of it.

The pivot engine and the designer are an Enterprise feature; the grid they sit on is MIT on npm. The same engine drives pivot over server data, where the server returns the aggregates and the browser never sees the detail rows, and it drives the pivot table inside the spreadsheet too. The docs page below has the configuration from all of this.

tutorials.title: Sankey, treemap and 29 chart types in Svelte
tutorials.description: A chart component for Svelte 5 with no charting dependency: hand it a plain spec and it draws inline SVG, from a bar chart to a sankey, treemap or sunburst.

transcript.text: Most Svelte component libraries stop before charts, and the ones that do charts usually wrap a large JavaScript charting library, which you then carry in your bundle, configure in its own vocabulary, and theme separately from everything else. This is neither. It is one component that takes a plain object describing what you want and draws inline SVG. Twenty nine types share that one object, including the three or four shapes that normally send people looking for a second dependency: the sankey, the treemap, the sunburst.

Here is the whole API. Import the chart component, describe the chart as data: a type, and the values it needs. This one is a sunburst, so the values are a hierarchy. There is no chart builder to learn and no plugin to register.
Nineteen lines, and no grid anywhere in it. The chart is a component in its own right, so it works on a dashboard, in a card, or beside a table you happen to have.

A sankey is the one people give up on. It takes a list of nodes and a list of links, works out the depth of each node by its longest path, and sizes every band by the value flowing through it. Change the data and the whole layout recomputes; there is nothing to position by hand and no coordinates in your source. That is the actual reason flow diagrams end up as a screenshot pasted into a slide: the drawing is the hard part, not the numbers. Here the numbers are the input and the drawing is the output.

A treemap is the same idea for a hierarchy: revenue by region, then category, then product, with area standing in for size. It is the chart that answers what is big and what is inside it in one picture, and it is the other one people reach for a separate library to get.

And when there is a grid in the picture, the chart can read its rows rather than a copy of them. That matters more than it sounds. The usual arrangement is a chart fed by its own query, which drifts from the table beside it the moment someone filters: two numbers on one screen that disagree, and an afternoon spent working out which one lied. Here the filter narrows the rows and the chart is drawing those rows, so the two cannot disagree.

Twenty nine types share that one spec, from the ordinary bar and line through to pareto, bullet, stream, nightingale and dumbbell. They render as inline SVG, so they print, they scale, and they carry text a screen reader can read. And when you do have a grid, the chart can read its rows directly, so filtering the table filters the chart. The types page below has a live example of every one.

tutorials.title: A tree grid in Svelte: hierarchies from flat rows
tutorials.description: Org charts, work breakdowns and permission trees from a flat array: name a parent field and the grid nests the rows, with totals, checkboxes and lazy loading.

transcript.text: Org charts, work breakdowns, folder trees, permission matrices. They all arrive from the database the same way: a flat list of rows where one column points at another row. Turning that into something a person can read is usually where the custom component gets written. It does not need to be.

Here is the whole thing. Rows with an id and a parent id, exactly as they came out of the query, and one prop that says which field is which. No pre-nesting, no building a tree of children arrays before you render, no recursive component.
The grid works out the depth of every row, draws the expanders, and keeps it a grid: the columns still sort, the cells still edit, and a child row is a row like any other.

Five levels of an employee hierarchy, chief executive down to individual contributors. Open a branch and the people under it appear. This is a grid rather than a diagram of boxes and lines, which is the right shape for a hierarchy you need to read numbers out of rather than frame on a wall.

The same structure carries behaviour down it. This is a permissions matrix: tick a workspace and every resource under it follows, untick one child and the parent goes to the indeterminate state rather than lying to you about what is selected. That tri-state is the detail people get wrong when they build this by hand.

If the tree is too big to send at once, the same prop works against a server: the grid asks for a branch when someone opens it, and nothing else travels. If you want the hierarchy as a picture rather than a table, the sunburst and the treemap chart types take the same shape of data. The docs page below has the flat array and the one prop from the start of this.

tutorials.title: A data grid in a SvelteKit app
tutorials.description: Add SvGrid to SvelteKit: rows from a +page.server.ts load, the grid in the page, and real server-rendered HTML rather than an empty shell.

transcript.text: In SvelteKit the data comes from a load function. SvGrid takes it as a plain array.
Add the package to an existing project, or scaffold the whole SvelteKit app from the template.
Query in the load function, on the server, where your database credentials already are.
Then the page takes the rows straight from data and hands them to the grid. Type the columns against your row type and every field is checked.
For a table too big to send at once, move sort, filter and paging to the server and the grid requests one page at a time.
The server HTML carries a viewport of real rows, so the page is useful before hydration. The SvelteKit guide is at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: A SvelteKit CRUD app from a database, in one command
tutorials.description: Point SvGrid Studio at a schema and it writes a SvelteKit app: a list, an edit form and a record page per table, as source you own and keep editing.

transcript.text: Every internal tool starts the same way. There are tables, somebody needs to see them and change them, and two weeks disappear into list screens and forms the same shape as the last ones you wrote.

This is the kind of thing people mean. A sales pipeline: every row a deal, every column a number somebody has to defend on Friday. Owners, stages, values, close dates, the lot. It is not hard work exactly, it is just a lot of it, and it looks the same in every company you have ever worked at.

So point the generator at where your data already lives. A Postgres or MySQL connection string, a Drizzle or Prisma schema file, an OpenAPI document, or for this one a sample dataset so you can follow along without a database. Pick a theme while you are there.
Twenty eight files, six screens, two tables. Install it and run it the way you would any SvelteKit project, because that is all it is.

And that is the app, in the theme you asked for. A nav built from your tables, a card per entity, and a working screen behind each one. Nothing here is a placeholder waiting for you to fill it in, and nothing is a component from a library you now depend on at runtime. It is routes, components and a schema file, in your repository.

The list screen is the grid you already know, wired to the schema: a column per field, a filter per column, paging at the bottom, and the types carried through from the table definition rather than retyped by hand. Which is the quiet part that matters. The schema file is one place, and the grid columns, the form controls and the validation all read from it. Add a field to the table and it appears in all three, instead of you remembering the three files that have to agree.

The manage screen pairs the list with an editor. Pick a record and its form appears underneath, built from the same schema: every field gets the control its type asks for, and the validation is that schema read back to you. Create and update are both already wired. This is the part that normally eats the fortnight.

The important part is what it is not. It is not a runtime you ship, and it is not a black box you configure forever. It is source in your repository, under your version control, which you edit like anything else you wrote. Re-run the generator and the parts you changed stay changed, because the generated regions are marked and the rest is left alone. Studio is the Suite tier; the grid it builds on is MIT on npm.

tutorials.title: One grid, twenty themes
tutorials.description: SvGrid themes are CSS custom properties, so the same grid wears your design system: twenty presets, light and dark, plus density and a live theme builder.

transcript.text: A grid that looks like a grid library is a grid that never ships. SvGrid is themed with CSS variables.
This is the same demo, the same markup, under four presets. Here is the signature one.
The same grid in a shadcn-flavoured palette. Nothing changed but the tokens.
Material, with its own density and radius.
And a spreadsheet look, for users who expect one.
Start from a preset or set the tokens yourself in the theme builder at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: What is SvGrid
tutorials.description: A data grid built for Svelte 5: a million rows, filters, inline editing, grouping, pivot mode, a Kanban board and charts, from one component.
tutorials.anchor: This guide is six short pages

transcript.text: SvGrid is a data grid written for Svelte 5. Not a port of something older and not a wrapper around it: runes and snippets the whole way down. Here is what it does.
It starts with scale. A million rows in the browser, virtualized in both directions, so the number of DOM nodes stays about the same as it was with ten.
Then the work people actually do with a table. Every column carries a filter menu listing the values that are in it, so narrowing the data is picking from a list.
Cells edit in place, with the editor each column asks for, and validation that refuses a value instead of writing it and cleaning up afterwards.
Group by any column and each group header carries its own totals, averaged or summed from the raw values rather than the formatted text.
The same component flips into pivot mode, and the rows become a cross-tab. There is no second library underneath and no export to a spreadsheet to get there.
Hand it the board prop and those rows become cards in lanes. Same data, same column definitions, and dragging a card writes back to the row.
Charts read off the grid's own rows, so whatever you filtered is what you plot, and the chart moves when the table does.
Twenty themes ship with the package, each carrying a light and a dark palette, and every surface underneath is a CSS custom property you can set yourself.
The AI helpers are in the free package rather than sold as an add-on, and they are model agnostic: you hand them a provider and ask for a filter in plain words.
The grid is MIT on npm, it server-renders in SvelteKit, and the docs carry a ten lesson video course that builds all of this from an empty project. Install it and see how far twenty lines get you.

tutorials.title: One grid, five views
tutorials.description: SvGrid renders the same rows as a table, a Kanban board, a calendar, a pivot table and a chart. Same data, same columns, one prop per view.

transcript.text: Most apps end up with a table, a board and a calendar over the same records, and three components to keep in sync. SvGrid has one.
The board prop turns rows into cards and a status field into lanes. Drag a card, and the row changes.
Switch to Table, and it is the same grid with the same rows, the moved card already in Review.
The scheduler prop renders the rows as a calendar: month, week, day and agenda, with drag to move and resize.
Pivot mode summarizes the same rows by any dimension, with a designer docked beside the grid.
And the charting prop draws what is on screen. Filter the grid, the chart follows; click the chart, the grid follows.
One data model, one set of columns, one component. The views are props. See them all at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Pivot designer in SvGrid
tutorials.description: Drag fields into the Rows, Columns and Values wells of SvPivotDesigner and watch the pivot grid recompute: a self-contained pivot builder for Svelte.

transcript.text: SvPivotDesigner is a pivot builder in one component: a field list on the left and drop wells for filters, columns, rows and values.
Drag Salesperson into the Rows well.
The pivot grid recomputes at once, one row per salesperson, with the measures summed across the columns.
Measures work the same way. Drop Profit into Values, and click its chip to switch the aggregator between sum, average, count and more.

tutorials.title: Pivot mode in SvGrid
tutorials.description: Dock the pivot designer beside a flat SvGrid with panelPosition right and flip Pivot mode: the same rows become a pivot table with heat-mapped measures.

transcript.text: With panelPosition set to right, the pivot designer docks beside the grid. The flat rows stay editable, sortable and filterable.
Flip the Pivot mode switch.
The same grid becomes a pivot table. Rows and columns come from the wells, and the measures are heat-mapped by value.
Flip it back, and the flat rows return with their state intact. One grid, two views, no second data source.

tutorials.title: A spreadsheet in your Svelte app
tutorials.description: The SvGrid spreadsheet shell: an Excel-style ribbon, a formula engine across sheets, conditional formatting, charts anchored to ranges, and xlsx in and out.

transcript.text: Sometimes a grid is not enough and what people want is a spreadsheet. SvGrid ships one.
SvSheet is the whole surface: a six-tab ribbon, the name box and formula bar, lettered columns and sheet tabs, with every Excel shortcut wired in.
One formula engine spans the workbook. Orders looks prices up from Products, and Summary adds it all up across sheets.
Conditional formatting is part of the document: data bars, colour scales and top-N rules over computed values, edited from the ribbon.
Charts anchor to ranges the way Excel anchors them. Change a number and the chart redraws; save, and it lands in the xlsx as a real chart.
Formulas, formats, charts and files, in a component your users already know how to use. Details at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: SvGrid Studio: from a database to an app
tutorials.description: Point SvGrid Studio at your tables and get a SvelteKit app: a searchable list, an edit form and a record page per table, from the CLI or the visual designer.

transcript.text: Every internal tool starts the same way: tables in a database, and the pages to browse and edit them. SvGrid Studio generates those pages.
From the terminal, init reads the tables and writes the app.
Or do it visually. The designer asks where the data is, which pages each table gets, and builds the app in the browser.
Screens are blocks on a canvas: a KPI, a chart, a grid, a form. Drag them around, bind them to data, add an action.
Preview runs it as your users will see it.
Generate app writes a real SvelteKit project: typed schemas, routes, a data layer and a CI workflow. Download it, or open it in StackBlitz. It is code, and it is yours.
Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, SQLite, Supabase, a REST endpoint or an OpenAPI spec. Try it at svgrid.com slash studio.

tutorials.title: SvGrid in 60 seconds
tutorials.description: The Svelte 5 data grid: a million rows, Excel-style filters, inline editing, pivot mode, a Kanban board and charts, all from one component.

transcript.text: This is SvGrid, a data grid written for Svelte 5. One component, sixty seconds.
It starts with scale. A million rows in the browser, virtualized, sorted, filtered and edited in place.
Filters work the way spreadsheet users expect: a menu on every column with a searchable value list.
Editing is one prop. Double-click, type, Enter. Text, numbers, dropdowns, dates and checkboxes each get the right editor.
Flip pivot mode and the same rows become a pivot table, with the designer docked beside them.
Or a Kanban board. Lanes come from a status field, and a drop writes the row back.
Charts read the rows on screen. Click a bar to filter the grid to that category.
The core is MIT. The pivot, board, charts and spreadsheet ship in the enterprise pack. Start at svgrid.com.

tutorials.title: Tree data in SvGrid
tutorials.description: Nest flat rows into an expandable hierarchy with the treeData prop: a parent field, a tree column, expanders with indent, and expand or collapse all.

transcript.text: Tree data is one prop. Point treeData at the parent field and name the tree column, and flat rows become a hierarchy.
Click an expander to open a branch. Children indent under their parent and keep every column.
Expand all and Collapse all walk the whole tree through the grid API.
Nested objects work too: flatten them once with flattenTreeData, and the same prop takes it from there.
